title: My Grandma's Sunday Gravy (Finally Written Down)
creator: Marco in the Kitchen
description:
It took me eleven years to get my grandmother to tell me the actual measurements. Here they are.

Ingredients:
2 lb pork shoulder
1 lb Italian sausage
2 cans San Marzano tomatoes
1 small can tomato paste
6 cloves garlic
Fresh basil, olive oil, salt, a parmesan rind

Thanks to First Pages for partnering on this video. They put books into the hands of kids who don't have any at home. Donate or volunteer: firstpages.org/marco

Recipe card: marcointhekitchen.com/gravy

sentences.t: Okay, this is the one, this is the recipe I've been promising you guys for, what, two years now?
My grandmother's Sunday gravy, and yes, in our family it's gravy, not sauce, please don't fight me in the comments.
And quick thing before I start browning meat, because once I start I can't stop.
This video is brought to you by First Pages, a nonprofit that I've actually wanted to work with for a long time.
They get books to kids who don't have any at home, like, literally zero books in the house, which is way more common than you'd think.
My grandma never finished school, and the first thing she did when she had grandkids was make sure we had a shelf full of books.
So when they reached out, it was an easy yes.
Every ten dollars puts about four new books in a kid's hands, picked for their age and their language.
If you want to donate, or sign up to volunteer at one of their reading days, go to firstpages.org slash marco, it's in the description.
Thank you to First Pages for sponsoring this one.
Alright, meat.
I've got about two pounds of pork shoulder here, cut into big chunks, like fist-sized.
And a pound of sausage, the sweet kind, she never used hot, she said hot sausage was for people who can't cook.
Salt everything, more than you think, and get your pot really hot with a good glug of olive oil.
Listen to that.
You want a proper crust on every side, don't move it around, just let it sit.
This is where a lot of the flavor comes from, all that brown stuff stuck to the bottom of the pot.
Okay, meat comes out, and now garlic, six cloves, just smashed, not chopped.
Her rule was, the second you can smell it from the next room, it's done.
Tomato paste goes in now, and you want to cook it until it goes from bright red to kind of brick colored.
That takes a couple minutes, keep stirring.
Now the tomatoes, two big cans, and I crush them with my hands, which is messy but it's the right way.
Rinse each can with a little water and dump that in too, she'd yell at me if I wasted any.
Meat goes back in, along with all the juices on the plate.
And the secret weapon, a parmesan rind, the hard end that you'd normally throw away.
It just melts in slowly and makes everything taste deeper and kind of savory.
A few basil leaves, torn, lid on but cracked a little, and now we wait.
How long, you ask, and this is where I finally got an actual answer out of her.
Four hours, at the lowest heat you can manage, stirring every half hour or so.
For years she just said, until it's ready, which is not helpful, Nonna.
Okay, four hours later, and look at the color on that.
It's gone dark and glossy, and the pork just falls apart if you touch it with a spoon.
Fish out the rind and the basil, taste for salt.
In our house the meat came out on a separate plate and the gravy went on the pasta, rigatoni, always rigatoni.
Little bit of pasta water to loosen it, toss it in the pot, and finish with way too much cheese.
Okay, let's try it.
Yeah, that's it, that's Sunday, that tastes exactly like being nine years old at her table.
The full recipe card with all the measurements is on my site, link's below.
And if you make it, please send me a picture, I'm going to show my grandma every single one.
Ciao, see you next week.
